lesson.title: Ethereum: A Computer, Not Just a Currency
lesson.summary: Ethereum extended the blockchain concept with a built-in programming environment, letting developers deploy self-executing smart contracts rather than restricting the ledger to simple payments.
lesson.body:
Ethereum was proposed by Vitalik Buterin and a group of collaborators and launched in 2015, building on the same core blockchain structure covered earlier in this unit, a chain of cryptographically linked blocks maintained by a decentralized network, but adding something Bitcoin deliberately left out: a built in, general purpose programming environment called the Ethereum Virtual Machine. Where a basic blockchain ledger just records who paid whom, Ethereum lets developers deploy smart contracts, pieces of code that live permanently on the chain and execute automatically according to rules written into them, with no company or server operator needed to run them afterward.

This is a genuine difference in kind, not just degree. Bitcoin's scripting language is intentionally limited and not Turing complete, meaning it cannot express arbitrary computation, largely to keep the network simple and predictable. Ethereum's execution environment is expressive enough, within limits described below, to implement arbitrary program logic, which is what makes it possible to build decentralized exchanges, lending platforms, digital collectibles, and voting systems as smart contracts whose code and current state are stored directly on the blockchain rather than on a company's private server.

That expressiveness needs a safeguard, since arbitrary code could otherwise run forever or be used to spam the network, and this is where Ether, Ethereum's native currency, does its real job. Every operation a smart contract performs costs a fee called gas, priced in Ether, paid by whoever sends the transaction that triggers it. This compensates the network's validators for the computation they perform and, just as importantly, forces every transaction to specify a gas limit; if execution runs out of gas before finishing, it halts and reverts, which prevents an accidental or malicious infinite loop from stalling the network indefinitely.

Ethereum's consensus mechanism has changed over its history in a way worth understanding clearly. It originally used proof of work, the same general approach as Bitcoin, where miners competed using computational effort to add new blocks. In September 2022, in an upgrade widely known as the Merge, Ethereum switched entirely to proof of stake, where validators lock up, or stake, Ether as collateral instead of burning electricity on mining, and can lose that stake if they act dishonestly. This cut the network's energy consumption dramatically and changed who can realistically participate in validating: capital committed as stake became the primary requirement, rather than specialized mining hardware.

One more structural detail distinguishes Ethereum from Bitcoin and matters for understanding how smart contracts work: Ethereum uses an account based ledger model, tracking a balance and, for contracts, a stored state directly per account, rather than Bitcoin's model of tracking discrete unspent transaction outputs. This makes it considerably more natural to represent the kind of ongoing, stateful logic a smart contract typically needs to maintain between transactions.
